title: 'They were all asleep': Ukrainians describe deadly overnight Russian apartment strike
originalTitle: 'They were all asleep': Ukrainians describe deadly overnight Russian apartment strike
content:
All that was left of Tetiana's flat after the Russian strike was one outer wall with a satellite dish still clinging to it.

A drone hit her apartment block in Dymer, near Kyiv, before dawn on Sunday, killing 11 of her neighbours.

Tetiana wasn't home. She spent the night in a nearby village, celebrating her 60th birthday.

"I have no flat any more. It's gone. What can I say?" she wondered the next day, as she stood among the anxious crowd gathered waiting for news of neighbours and relatives. "Yesterday was my birthday – so today it's like I've been born again."

The bodies of the victims, including a teenager, have now been pulled from the ruins.

A whole section of the five-storey block was destroyed, collapsing into a mound of rubble which rescuers climbed to search for survivors.

On Sunday evening, they managed to find a seven-year-old boy, Davyd, alive and able to direct them to where he was trapped.

He's now being cared for in hospital, as well as Valentyna, a 79-year-old woman who was rescued almost a full day after the deadly strike. Caught between concrete slabs, still in her bed, she too had managed to call the emergency teams towards her.

Two residents of the building are still officially missing, though most of the wreckage has now been cleared.

The Russian attack happened as Ukrainian naval drones sank a Russian warship, the Merkury, which had docked for refuelling in Libya. The Angara cargo ship, which Kyiv says is used for military logistics and is on US and Ukrainian sanctions lists, was also hit.

"We are responding to Russia's aggression," President Volodymyr Zelensky said, calling both vessels legitimate targets.

He said the block of flats in Dymer, a village in the Kyiv region, had been struck by a Russian Shahed drone, possibly one of the jet-powered drones that travel at extremely high speeds and have been launched at Ukraine in large numbers in recent days.

Zelensky stressed that such weapons used foreign components, and he called for sanctions to be tightened.

"Every country and every leader who helps maintain pressure on the aggressor helps protect human life," he said.

But even hours after the initial attack, the danger had not passed.

Russia increasingly uses its drones to hit Ukraine just as rescuers go to work. They're known as "double-tap" attacks, and often deadly.

It makes the work of searching for survivors, which now happens every single day, extremely perilous.

In Dymer, all rescue work had to stop multiple times on Sunday as more Russian drones were detected overhead.

The emergency services, as well as residents and the press, had only moments to clear the scene and rush for shelter as Ukrainian fighter jets began shooting drones out of the sky.

Many people huddled in an underground kindergarten, decked out with children's paintings and balloons, the safest place around.

In one corner, we found its director crouching on a tiny child's chair.

Natalia had rushed to the scene minutes after hearing the explosion just after 05:00.

"I know all the children," she told us.

One of them, 12-year-old Kira, was later confirmed to have been killed together with her mother.

"So many people," Natalia said quietly. "It happened at night. Had it been daytime, then people might have been out at work. Or the shops. But they were all asleep."

At one point, a mother - held up by emergency workers - directed rescuers towards her son. "Go gently," she urged them, as they carried him out on a stretcher.

But 18-year-old Roman didn't make it.

He had only come home on Saturday night to collect some papers for college, his cousin said. He wasn't even supposed to be here.

The number of civilians casualties here has been surging in recent weeks.

On Sunday, in the Kyiv region alone, four people were killed in two other deadly attacks - one on a supermarket. A young teacher was among the dead.

"This is the tactic of Russian Federation," Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration told us at the scene. "They are trying to make us scared. To stop Ukraine fighting. But they cannot do this with us."

But the aerial attacks - and retaliation - are now almost non-stop and their scope is widening.

Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk, Marianne Baisnée and Matthew Goddard
